title: Home Geography for Primary Grades
author: C. C. Long
licenseEvidence: Project Gutenberg eBook #12228: public domain in the USA; American Book Company textbook published around the turn of the century (well before 1930) First published by American Book Company in 1894.
description: A gentle classic primer that teaches geography by starting at your own front door: finding north by the sun and stars, measuring and mapping your room, and spotting hills, streams, and ponds nearby. Each sitting is one or two short lessons with a hands-on or outdoor activity, a poem now and then, and a few questions to talk over. Great for siblings together, and the full text is free online.
includes: 31 sittings covering all 45 lessons, in 5 units
Link to the free full text for every lesson
Hands-on activities from the book: shadow watching, room plans, sand-table land forms, water experiments
Questions with answers for each sitting
Covers direction, maps, land and water forms, weather, plants, animals, minerals, and how people work

units.title: Unit 1: Direction, Distance, and Plans (Lessons I–X)

lessons.title: Lessons I–II: Position; How the Sun Shows Direction
steps: Read Lessons I and II together and do the right/left/front/back game at the table, then turn around and play it again
Go outside in the morning and point to where the sun rose; name that direction east
Stand with your right arm toward east and left arm toward west, and name north (in front) and south (behind)
Copywork: copy the sentence about the sun rising in the east and setting in the west
questions: In which direction does the sun seem to rise?
In which direction does it seem to set?
If your right hand points east and your left hand points west, which way are you facing?
lessons.notes: Right and left change when you turn around; north, south, east, and west don't. That is the big idea of these first lessons.

lessons.title: Lessons III–IV: How the Stars Show Direction; How the Compass Shows Direction
steps: Read Lessons III and IV together
On a clear night, go outside and find the Big Dipper; follow its two pointer stars to the North Star
Look at a real compass (or a phone compass) and watch the needle settle; mark N, S, E, W on paper around it
Draw the eight points of the compass: N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW
questions: Which star always shows the north?
What is the name of the group of stars that contains the Dipper?
Which direction is halfway between north and east?

lessons.title: Lessons V–VI: Questions on Direction; What the Winds Bring (poem)
steps: Read Lesson V and talk through the questions together
Mark where your shadow falls at three times of day (morning, noon, and late afternoon); notice when it is shortest
Look for a flag, smoke, or weather vane and decide which way the wind is blowing
Read the poem "What the Winds Bring" (Lesson VI) aloud and talk about what each wind brings
questions: When during the day is your shadow shortest?
In what direction will birds fly when winter comes?
In the poem, what does the north wind bring?
answers: At noon, when the sun is highest
Snowflakes (and frost pictures on the windows)

lessons.title: Lesson VII: How to Tell Distance
steps: Read Lesson VII together
Measure with a ruler: a book, a table, and a doorway; then use a yardstick or tape measure on a room
Guess a distance by eye (like across the yard), then measure it to check
Talk about a place about a mile from home and how long it would take to walk there
questions: How many inches are in a foot?
How many feet are in a yard?
Which measure is used for long distances, like between towns?
lessons.notes: The book suggests guessing first, then measuring, and repeating until the guesses get close.

lessons.title: Lesson VIII: Pictures and Plans
steps: Read Lesson VIII together and compare the picture and the plan of the schoolroom
Trace around blocks on paper to make a plan of a block 'house', like the boy in the lesson
Begin a plan of one room at home: measure two walls and choose a scale, such as 1 inch for 1 foot
questions: What is the difference between a picture and a plan?
In the lesson's plan, what does one inch stand for?
answers: A picture shows things as we see them; a plan shows where things are and their direction from each other

lessons.title: Lessons IX–X: Written Exercise; God Made Them All (poem)
steps: Read Lesson IX and answer the questions about your own home or school in full sentences
Draw a plan of your room at home with the bed, table, chairs, and door; mark N, S, E, and W
Draw a plan of your house and yard
Read the poem "God Made Them All" (Lesson X) aloud
questions: What do we call a drawing that shows where things are in a room?
Is the top of a plan always north?
answers: No; you have to mark which way is north

units.title: Unit 2: Land Forms and Weather (Lessons XI–XVII)

lessons.title: Lesson XI: Plains
steps: Read Lesson XI together
Find the flattest piece of land near you and imagine it stretching for miles; that is a plain
Find a picture of a palm tree and draw it
Talk about why travelers cross the desert on camels instead of horses
questions: What is a broad, nearly level stretch of land called?
What is a grassy, flowery plain called?
What is an oasis?
answers: A fertile spot with water in the middle of a desert

lessons.title: Lesson XII: Hills, Mountains, Valleys
steps: Read Lesson XII together
Walk up a hill (or the biggest slope nearby) and name its base, slope, and summit; look at the view from the top
Model hills, mountains, and a valley in sand, clay, or play dough
Draw a hill you have seen, with a little of the land around it
questions: What do we call the bottom, the sides, and the top of a hill?
What is the land between hills or mountains called?
Is it warmer or colder at the top of a high mountain?
answers: The base (foot), the slopes (sides), and the summit (top)

lessons.title: Lessons XIII–XIV: Rain, Wind, and Snow; How Water Is Changed to Vapor
steps: Read Lessons XIII and XIV together
Wipe a damp sponge across a slate or chalkboard and watch the water disappear
Set a plate of water in the sun and check it later; talk about where the water went
With a grown-up, watch a kettle boil and see the water turn to vapor
questions: What does heat change water into?
Can warm air or cold air hold more vapor?
Why does vapor rise into the air?
lessons.notes: The book says to give the weather lessons when that weather happens; save a rainy or snowy day for these if you can.

lessons.title: Lesson XV: How Vapor Is Changed to Water
steps: Read Lesson XV together
With a grown-up, hold a cold plate over steaming water and watch drops form and roll down
Fill a glass or pitcher with ice water and watch mist and drops gather on the outside
Breathe on a cold window and see your breath turn to water
questions: What turns vapor back into water?
Where does the water on the outside of an ice-water pitcher come from?
Does the water come through the pitcher from inside?
answers: From vapor in the air that is cooled by the cold pitcher

lessons.title: Lessons XVI–XVII: Dew, Clouds, and Rain; The Fairy Artist (poem)
steps: Read Lesson XVI together
Go outside early in the morning to look for dew on the grass (or frost in cold weather)
Watch the clouds for a few minutes and notice how they change shape
Read the poem "The Fairy Artist" (Lesson XVII) and draw a frosty window picture
questions: What is dew?
What is frozen dew called?
What are clouds made of?
answers: Water from the air that cools on cold grass and leaves and turns into drops
Tiny drops of water or crystals of ice

units.title: Unit 3: Rivers, Maps, and Water Forms (Lessons XVIII–XXVIII)

lessons.title: Lesson XVIII: How Rivers Are Made
steps: Read Lesson XVIII together
Visit a brook, creek, or river if you can; notice which way the water flows and what grows on its banks
Draw a spring with a little brook flowing from it, and the grasses around it
Copywork: copy two of the river words (spring, source, mouth, tributary) with their meanings
questions: What is the beginning of a river called?
Where a river flows into another body of water is called its what?
What is a small stream flowing into a larger one called?

lessons.title: Lessons XIX–XX: More About Rivers; The Brook (poem)
steps: Read Lesson XIX together
Pour water slowly onto the ridge of a tent-shaped piece of paper or a sand ridge and watch it run down both sides (a water-parting)
Read the poem "The Brook" (Lesson XX) aloud and trace the brook's journey with your finger in the air
Talk about why a river runs fast in some places and slow in others
questions: What do we call hills that divide the water to flow down two sides?
What is it called when a river falls over a high ledge of rock?
Why does a river wind about on level land?
answers: The water moves slowly there and is easily turned from its course

lessons.title: Lesson XXI: Work of Flowing Rivers
steps: Read Lesson XXI together
Put mud and water in a jar, shake it, and let it stand; notice which settles first, the coarse or the fine
After a rain, look for little streams carrying soil down a slope
Collect a few smooth stones from a stream or beach and talk about how they got round
questions: What happens to muddy water when it stands still?
What makes stream stones smooth and round?
Where do rich river meadows come from?
answers: The mud settles to the bottom and the water clears
Rubbing against each other as the water rolls them along
Soil that rivers wash down from the hills and leave when they flood

lessons.title: Lessons XXII–XXIII: Waterdrop's Story; The River (poem)
steps: Read "Waterdrop's Story" (Lesson XXII) aloud
Narration: your child tells the waterdrop's whole journey back, from sea to cloud to rain to river to sea
Draw the water cycle as a circle of pictures
Read the poem "The River" (Lesson XXIII) and talk about its questions
questions: Where did the waterdrop's journey begin and end?
What made the drops come together and fall as rain?
What machine did the water turn on its way?
answers: The cold wind by the mountain chilled them and made them heavy

lessons.title: Lesson XXIV: A Map
steps: Read Lesson XXIV together
Draw a simple map with mountains (short facing lines) and a river (a line that gets thicker toward its mouth)
Look at a real map of your area and find a river, hills, and your town
questions: What is the difference between a plan and a map?
Why is the river line drawn thicker toward its mouth?
answers: A plan shows a room, house, or yard; a map shows land and water
Because the river gets wider as it flows toward the sea
lessons.notes: The book's warning is worth repeating: the lines on a map stand for real mountains and rivers, so picture the real thing.

lessons.title: Lesson XXV: Forms of Land and Water
steps: Read Lesson XXV together
Make a lake with an inlet, an outlet, and an island in sand, a sandbox, or a baking pan
If there is a pond or lake nearby, walk along part of its shore
Draw a map of a river and lake on paper
questions: What is a lake?
What is the river that lets water into a lake called?
What is an island?
answers: Water surrounded by land (a hollow in the land filled with water)
A piece of land with water all around it

lessons.title: Lesson XXVI: More About Forms of Land and Water
steps: Read Lesson XXVI together
In sand or after a rain, make a peninsula, an isthmus, a bay, and a strait
Look for pictures of bays and peninsulas in books or magazines
Copywork: copy the meaning of peninsula and strait
questions: What does the word peninsula mean?
What connects a peninsula to the mainland?
What is a strait?
answers: A narrow passage of water joining two larger bodies of water

lessons.title: Lessons XXVII–XXVIII: A Trip to the Highlands; Spring (poem)
steps: Read "A Trip to the Highlands" (Lesson XXVII) aloud
Take a walk to the highest place you can reach nearby and look for land and water forms from the top
Narration: your child retells the trip and names every land or water form the children saw
Read the poem "Spring" (Lesson XXVIII) aloud
questions: Did it get warmer or cooler as the children climbed?
What did the father say the land reaching out into the lake was?
How did the city look from the top of the hill?
answers: Small, with little straight streets and tiny house-tops

lessons.title: Lessons XXIX–XXX: Useful Vegetables; Useful Grains
steps: Read Lessons XXIX and XXX together
Sort vegetables from your kitchen: which do we eat the roots, leaves, stems, or seeds of?
Plant a few seeds (beans or corn) in a cup of soil and start watching them grow
Draw one of the grains, such as wheat or an ear of corn
questions: Name a vegetable whose root we eat.
Which grain makes the choicest flour?
Why is it called Indian corn?
answers: Any of: beet, turnip, radish, carrot
Because American Indians first raised it
lessons.notes: The book suggests planting seeds and watching them sprout; keep the cup going for the plant lessons that follow.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXI: Fruits
steps: Read Lesson XXXI together
Name fruits that grow near you and sort them: trees, bushes, or vines
Visit an orchard, garden, or market and look at where fruits come from
Talk about why people in hot and cold countries eat different foods
questions: What is a place where many fruit trees grow called?
Where does the orange grow in our country?
Name a fruit that grows on a vine.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXII: Useful Plants
steps: Read Lesson XXXII together
Look at the labels on your clothes and find which are cotton or linen
Find out where your sugar comes from; taste a little maple syrup if you have some
Write or tell what you learned about cotton and linen
questions: What plant does linen come from?
What machine separates cotton from its seeds?
Name two plants that sugar is made from.
answers: Sugar cane and the sugar maple

lessons.title: Lesson XXXIII: Forest Trees
steps: Read Lesson XXXIII together
Take a walk and learn the names of three trees near you; collect a leaf from each
Look at the wooden furniture in your home and guess what kinds of wood it is made of
Draw and color one of the trees you found
questions: What do we call trees planted along streets to keep off the sun?
How tall are some of the great trees of California?
What is lumber used for?

lessons.title: Lesson XXXIV: Flowers
steps: Read Lesson XXXIV together
Go on a flower walk and name as many flowers as you can; notice where each one grows
Find the parts of a plant: root, stem, leaves, bud, and flower
Begin learning the poem "Spring and the Flowers" by heart
questions: Name the parts of a plant.
Do all flowers grow in the same kind of place?
answers: Root, stem, leaves, bud, and flower
No; some need wet places and some need dry ones

lessons.title: Lessons XXXV–XXXVI: What Is Necessary to Make Plants Grow; Summer Rain (poem)
steps: Read Lesson XXXV together
Check on your seed cup: talk about what it needs to keep growing
Try an experiment: keep one seedling in the dark or without water and compare it with one that has light and water
Read the poem "Summer Rain" (Lesson XXXVI) aloud
questions: What two things does the lesson say plants need to grow?
Why don't plants grow in deserts?
Why don't plants grow in winter?

units.title: Unit 5: Animals, Minerals, and People (Lessons XXXVII–XLV)

lessons.title: Lessons XXXVII–XXXVIII: The Parts of Animals; The Covering of Animals
steps: Read Lessons XXXVII and XXXVIII together
Watch a cat, dog, chicken, or duck and notice its feet, claws, beak, or bill and what it uses them for
Draw a duck's webbed foot next to a hen's foot
Sort animals by their covering: fur, hair, feathers, wool, scales, or shell
questions: What do we call animals that live near people and are tame?
What keeps a duck's feathers from getting wet?
Why does a duck have webbed feet?
lessons.notes: The big idea of both lessons: each animal has the parts and the covering that suit the life it leads.

lessons.title: Lessons XXXIX–XL: Uses of Animals; The Signs of the Seasons (poem)
steps: Read Lesson XXXIX together
Find things at home that come from animals: wool, leather, milk, eggs, silk
Make a list of animals that are useful for food, for work, and for clothing
Read the poem "The Signs of the Seasons" (Lesson XL) and look outside for signs of the season you are in now
questions: Where does wool come from?
How is silk made?
In the poem, what are two signs that spring is here?
answers: Silkworms spin cocoons of silk thread
The bluebird comes and builds its nest, and violets peep up

lessons.title: Lesson XLI: Things Found in the Earth
steps: Read Lesson XLI together
Hunt around the house for things made of iron or steel, copper, tin, brass, and gold or silver
Look at a pencil and talk about what the 'lead' is really made of
Start a collection of rocks and minerals from your area, as the book suggests
questions: What is the most useful of all metals, according to the lesson?
What is the hole dug in the earth to get minerals called?
What is a 'lead' pencil really made of?

lessons.title: Lesson XLII: More About Things Found in the Earth
steps: Read Lesson XLII together
Walk around your neighborhood and look for granite, marble, slate, brick, and sandstone in buildings, steps, and curbs
Rub a piece of sandstone or chalk to see how it crumbles; compare it with a hard stone
Add any building stones you find to your rock collection and label them
questions: What is the place where building stone is dug called?
What are bricks made from?
What is glass made from?

lessons.title: Lesson XLIII: How People Live, and What They Are Doing
steps: Read Lesson XLIII together
Talk about the kinds of homes people live in: tents, wigwams, huts, snow houses, bamboo houses
Trace one thing you ate today back to the plant or animal it came from
Name the work of farmers, stock-raisers, miners, lumbermen, and fishermen
questions: What do we call the work of raising crops?
What is the business of raising cows and sheep called?
When do lumbermen cut trees, and how do the logs get to the mill?
answers: In winter; they float down the streams in spring when the snow melts

lessons.title: Lessons XLIV–XLV: More About What People Are Doing; A Review Lesson
steps: Read Lessons XLIV and XLV together
Make a list of all the jobs (occupations) you can think of, and the jobs people do near you
Pick one thing in your home and talk about where it was made and how it got to you
Review: walk through your town or neighborhood and name the stores, workshops, roads, or waterways you see
questions: What do we call the buying, selling, and exchanging of goods?
Where are most things made in a city?
Why do people in different places do different kinds of work?
answers: It depends on the place they live: the land, mountains, sea, or city around them
